source.title: Disentangling the Mechanisms Behind Implicit Regularization in SGD
source.authors: Zachary Novack; Simran Kaur; Tanya Marwah; S. Garg; Zachary Chase Lipton

record.tranche_reason: Tests large-batch generalization gaps and whether explicit regularization or other training changes recover small-batch performance, using test accuracy and gradient-norm trajectories.
record.gate_note: Rows below report this study’s own test-accuracy comparisons and gradient-norm measurements. Cited findings from prior work are excluded. Hyperparameter values used only to tune experiments are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures small-versus-large-batch test accuracy and tests recipe changes that reduce the gap, bearing on V5. Its fixed-update and training-accuracy stopping rules do not test V5's fixed-epoch premise.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that small-micro-batch gradient-norm and Fisher-trace penalties can substantially recover small-batch generalization, whereas Jacobian penalties do not. Recovery weakens with larger micro-batches. Similar gradient-norm trajectories correlate with recovery but are not necessary. Grafting and NGD work much better on CIFAR10 than CIFAR100. The headline recovery wording should retain the incomplete results and Appendix A.5's sample-regularization qualification for Tiny-ImageNet.
record.recipe_differences: Uses fixed-iteration small- versus large-batch SGD with explicit gradient-norm, Fisher-trace and Jacobian penalties, and evaluates other large-batch training changes. The listed claim versions describe other studies and recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset (CIFAR10 versus CIFAR100 and other image datasets); micro-batch size; regularizer type; training method (grafting/NGD); added momentum, weight decay and cosine schedule.

fits_no_version.finding: Gradient-norm trajectory similarity often accompanies recovery, but grafting and NGD can approach small-batch accuracy without matching that trajectory.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Matching small-batch gradient-norm trajectories is associated with, but not necessary for, large-batch generalization recovery.

record.problems: Main test-accuracy results average two to three initializations. The authors acknowledge that progressively finer hyperparameter tuning could improve performance. Experiments use image benchmarks and fixed update iterations; the specified language and fixed-epoch conditions are not tested.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Figure-only gradient-norm trajectories are not transcribed as numerical rows; the text describes their patterns, and Figure 1 and Figure 2 locators are given in the excerpts.

untested.parts: Fixed random-label fitting and its comparison with natural-label held-out accuracy.
Width sweeps and generalization beyond the width needed for interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and learned local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.

Equal-epoch batch comparisons; language models; identification of a workload-dependent batch threshold; longer-training, learning-rate-scaling and warmup remedies; controlled normalization changes. Fixed update counts do not demonstrate recovery within the same epoch budget.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on training-set size or augmentation.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation sharpness, generalization-gap rankings, and comparisons with norm or margin measures.
Removal of memorized examples versus random removal.

missing.what: External grafting results are missing because r34–r37 actually contain iterative grafting. External grafting accuracies are 92.12 and 88.65 on CIFAR10, and 68.3 and 59.71 on CIFAR100 for ResNet18 and VGG16 respectively. They support near recovery on CIFAR10 and qualify recovery on CIFAR100.

Additional VGG11/CIFAR10 regularizer comparison: SB 78.19, LB 73.90, GN 77.62, FT 79.10, AJ 74.09; UJ unavailable. FT exceeds the small-batch reference, GN reduces the gap, and AJ retains it. GN differs from Table 3's 76.89 without an explained reason.

Sample micro-batch regularization accuracy results are omitted, beyond the declared omission of gradient-norm trajectories. The text reports near or better small-batch accuracy with suitable settings, diminishing benefits with larger sampled micro-batches, and similar final performance to average regularization on CIFAR100 and VGG11/CIFAR10. Exact values require reading the plots.

Anti-PGD on ResNet18/CIFAR100 fails to recover the 71.21 small-batch reference: the six reported test accuracies are 67.54, 65.44, 64.55, 64.90, 62.52 and 62.78. These qualify this particular noise-based recovery recipe.

record.verdict_notes: States consistently describe the remaining large-batch accuracy penalty: observed means it persists, partial means it is reduced, and absent means it is removed or described as recovered. Baseline small-batch rows inherit their paired comparison's state. Failure of a particular remedy does not challenge V5's qualified claim that some adaptations can help. No challenges verdict is warranted. The record's ICLR 2022 publication attribution is not established by the supplied November 2022 preprint.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
Language models; fixed-epoch comparisons; effects of normalization changes; batches beyond a workload-dependent size. The main comparisons use fixed update iterations and image classifiers.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- or margin-based generalization measures.

relation.reason: The study measures small- versus large-batch held-out accuracy and tests interventions intended to close that gap.

tranche.reason: Explicit regularization, grafting and normalized gradient descent test the batch-generalization question through different methods. The study bears on recipe adaptation without directly testing the fixed-epoch premise.

source_check.notes: Equal-update and training-accuracy stopping experiments do not establish V5's fixed-epoch premise. Table 3 reports VGG11 GN accuracy 76.89 (±0.72), while Table 5 reports 77.62 for nominally similar training without explaining the difference.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: ResNet-18 on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, Tiny-ImageNet and SVHN; VGG11 on CIFAR10, micro-batch size 128 or 100
reader_labels.reason: Small-batch SGD exceeds large-batch SGD, while GN or FT often improves large-batch accuracy and FT matches or exceeds the small-batch result on CIFAR100, Tiny-ImageNet, and SVHN (r1–r4, r7–r10, r13–r16, r19–r22, r29–r31).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Larger micro-batches, CIFAR10 GN/FT results, and CIFAR100 grafting/NGD
reader_labels.reason: Recovery is incomplete on CIFAR10, worsens as micro-batch size grows, and grafting or NGD results that close the gap on CIFAR10 do not recover it on CIFAR100 (r3–r4, r25–r28, r34–r41).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: ResNet-18 on CIFAR100 with Jacobian regularization
reader_labels.reason: Average Jacobian regularization is below the large-batch SGD result and unit Jacobian regularization is approximately unchanged from it (r11–r12).
